content: Tubers are specialized plant structures that have undergone modification to store nutrients. These structures enable plants to survive through winter and regrow in subsequent years, as well as facilitate asexual reproduction. Tubers are categorized into two main types: stem tubers and root tubers. Stem Tubers Stem tubers develop from thickened rhizomes or stolons. The upper or lateral parts of the tuber generate shoots that grow into stems and leaves, while the lower parts produce roots. These tubers typically form near the soil surface, adjacent to the parent plant. A stem tuber serves as a temporary storage and regenerative organ, originating from a shoot that branches off a mature plant. New tubers, or offspring tubers, either remain attached to the parent tuber or form at the end of a hypogeogenous rhizome. During the fall, the parent plant dies, leaving behind the new tubers, which contain a dominant bud. In spring, this bud produces a new shoot that grows stems and leaves. By summer, the old tubers decay, and new ones begin to develop. Some plants produce smaller tubers or tubercles that function like seeds, giving rise to small plants resembling seedlings. While certain stem tubers, such as those of tuberous begonias, are long-lived, many tuberous plants have tubers that only persist until the plant has fully developed its leaves. At this point, the tuber shrivels and becomes non-functional. Stem tubers generally originate from the enlargement of the hypocotyl section of a seedling, though they may also include the first one or two nodes of the epicotyl and the upper root section. These tubers are vertically oriented, with vegetative buds at the top and fibrous roots at the basal section. They are typically oblong or rounded in shape. Examples of stem tubers include tuberous begonias and Cyclamen. The mignonette vine (Anredera cordifolia) produces aerial stem tubers on tall vines, which detach and grow upon falling to the ground. Another example is Plectranthus esculentus from the mint family (Lamiaceae), which forms underground tubers weighing up to 1.8 kg. These tubers develop from axillary buds that produce short stolons, which subsequently grow into tubers. Potatoes Potato tubers are specialized, swollen stems that develop from enlarged stolons. These tubers exhibit all the structural features of a typical stem, including nodes and internodes. The nodes, commonly referred to as eyes, are arranged in a spiral pattern around the tuber and contain leaf scars. The terminal bud is located at the end farthest from the stolon attachment, demonstrating apical dominance similar to a normal stem. Internally, potato tubers are composed of starch stored in enlarged parenchyma cells. They also contain the typical cellular structures of stems, such as a pith, vascular zones, and a cortex. Potato tubers are formed within a single growing season and serve as storage organs to help the plant survive through winter and propagate. When the above-ground parts of the plant die in the fall, the tubers remain underground and regenerate new shoots in the spring. These shoots utilize the stored nutrients in the tuber to grow. As the main shoot develops, it produces adventitious roots at its base and lateral buds along its length. The shoot also generates stolons, which are elongated stems that grow during long days under the influence of auxins and high gibberellin levels, which inhibit root formation on the stolons. Before tuber formation begins, the stolons must reach a certain developmental stage. The hormone lipoxygenase plays a role in regulating potato tuber development. When grown from seed, potato plants produce stolons near the soil surface. Tubers form close to the soil surface and may even develop above ground. During cultivation, potato tubers are often cut into pieces and planted deeper in the soil. This deeper planting allows for more space to generate larger tubers. The planted pieces sprout shoots that grow to the surface, producing rhizome-like structures and short stolons underground. Once the shoots reach the surface, they develop roots and grow into the green plant. It is important to distinguish stem tubers from tuberous roots (root tubers), such as sweet potatoes or dahlias. Stem tubers are modified stems, while root tubers are modified roots. Root Tubers Root tubers, also known as tuberous roots, are modified lateral roots that have become enlarged to function as storage organs. Although they share a similar appearance and function with stem tubers, their origin is distinct. Examples of plants with root tubers include sweet potatoes, cassava, and dahlias. These structures enable plants to survive from one year to the next by storing nutrients. Unlike true tubers, root tubers lack nodes, internodes, and reduced leaves. The proximal end of a root tuber contains crown tissue, which produces buds that grow into stems and foliage. The distal end typically produces unmodified roots. In contrast, true tubers exhibit the opposite arrangement, with the distal end producing stems. Root tubers are biennial in nature. During the first year, the parent plant produces the root tubers, and the above-ground parts of the plant die in the fall. In the second year, the root tubers generate a new plant, consuming their stored nutrients to produce new roots, stems, and flowers. Once this process is complete, the remaining tissue of the root tuber dies, while the plant generates new root tubers for the following year. An example of a plant with root tubers is Hemerocallis fulva (commonly known as the orange daylily), as well as various daylily hybrids. These plants spread via underground stolons that terminate in new fans, which grow roots and produce thick root tubers. These tubers then send out additional stolons. Plants with root tubers are typically propagated between late summer and late winter by digging up the tubers, separating them (ensuring each piece contains crown tissue), and replanting them.
